When a planet is found by the radial-velocity method, its orbital inclination i is unknown and can range from 0 to 90 degrees. The method is unable to determine the true mass (M) of the planet, but rather gives a lower limit for its mass, M sini. It has an extremely eccentric orbit like a comet, with its orbit taking it very close to its star and then back out very far away from it every 111 days. The variable radial velocity of HD 80606 was first noticed in 1999 from observations with the 10-m Keck 1 telescope at the W.

HD 209458 b is an exoplanet that orbits the solar analog HD 209458 in the constellation Pegasus, some 157 light-years (48 parsecs) from the Solar System. The radius of the planet's orbit is 0.047 AU (7.0 million km; 4.4 million mi), or one-eighth the radius of Mercury's orbit (0.39 AU (36 million mi; 58 million km)). This small radius results in a year that is 3.5 Earth-days long and an estimated surface temperature of about 1,000 °C (1,800 °F; 1,300 K). Its mass is 220 times that of Earth (0.69 Jupiter masses) and its volume is some 2.5 times greater than that of Jupiter.

We carried out a Bayesian homogeneous determination of the orbital parameters of 231 transiting giant planets (TGPs) that are alone or have distant companions; we employed differential evolution Markov chain Monte Carlo methods to analyse radial-velocity (RV) data from the literature and 782 new high-accuracy RVs obtained with the HARPS-N spectrograph for 45 systems over 3 years. Our work yields the largest sample of systems with a transiting giant exoplanet and coherently determined orbital, planetary, and stellar parameters. We found that the orbital parameters of TGPs in non-compact planetary systems are clearly shaped by tides raised by their host stars. Indeed, the most eccentric planets have relatively large orbital separations and/or high mass ratios, as expected from the equilibrium tide theory.

Following its initial detection through radial-velocity measurements with the HARPS spectrograph in 2008, subsequent observations have refined the orbital parameters of HD 40307 d using additional high-precision radial-velocity data. Analyses incorporating HARPS data spanning 2004 to 2012 confirmed the planet's signal and improved the precision of its orbital period to 20.4185 ± 0.0052 days and minimum mass to 8.74 ± 0.58 Earth masses, while accounting for stellar activity effects through Bayesian modeling.[4] A reanalysis in 2020 integrated new radial-velocity measurements from 2015 to 2017, further enhancing period precision and supporting the planet's existence within a multi-planet architecture, though it rejected signals for some outer candidates in the system.[15] Searches for transits of HD 40307 d have yielded non-detections, constraining its physical properties.
